rounds.statement: A coffee bean is actually the seed of a fruit
rounds.explain: True — it is the seed of the coffee cherry.

rounds.statement: Most of the world's coffee grows in a band near the equator
rounds.explain: True — the "bean belt" runs roughly 25°N to 25°S.

rounds.statement: Espresso beans are a special species grown only for espresso
rounds.explain: False — espresso is a brewing method, not a species. Any bean can be pulled as espresso.

rounds.statement: A coffee cherry usually contains two seeds
rounds.explain: True — two flat-faced seeds sit pressed together inside each cherry. Roughly one in twenty grows a single round seed instead: a peaberry.

rounds.statement: Robusta has less caffeine than Arabica
rounds.explain: False — Robusta has almost twice the caffeine of Arabica.

rounds.statement: Dark roasts always have far more caffeine than light roasts
rounds.explain: False — roast level barely changes caffeine; by volume light roasts can edge ahead.

rounds.statement: Dark roasts pack far more caffeine than light roasts
rounds.explain: False — roasting barely touches caffeine. It trades origin acidity for roast flavour, not stimulant for strength.

rounds.statement: Beans get bigger but lighter as they roast
rounds.explain: True — heat drives water out while steam pressure puffs the bean up. Lighter in weight, larger in size.

rounds.statement: Light roasts keep more of the origin’s own flavour
rounds.explain: True — the further a roast goes, the more roast flavour replaces what the farm put in.

rounds.statement: Shiny, oily beans are a sign of a fresh roast
rounds.explain: False — surface oil means a dark roast, an aging bag, or both. Freshness is on the roast date, not the shine.

rounds.statement: First crack is the landmark — light roasts stop soon after it
rounds.explain: True — the pop around 195–205 °C marks the start of drinkable roast levels; light roasts end shortly past it, dark roasts push on toward second crack.

rounds.statement: Coffee tastes best brewed the day it was roasted
rounds.explain: False — fresh-roasted beans are still venting CO₂, which fights the water. Most coffee peaks a few days to a month after roasting.

rounds.scenario: Grind’s dialled in and the beans are fresh.
rounds.prompt: The first sip puckers, and the cup feels hollow. What first?
rounds.explain: Puckering with no weight behind it is the under-extracted signature: the water left before it took enough. Finer grounds slow it down and pull the sweetness through.

rounds.scenario: Same beans, same ratio as the last cup.
rounds.prompt: This one dries your tongue and the bitterness lingers. What first?
rounds.explain: A drying finish that hangs around is the over-extracted signature — too much came out, including the harsh end of it. Coarser grounds ease the pull back toward balance.

rounds.scenario: You brewed it at 1:18. Nothing about it is sour.
rounds.prompt: Clean, pleasant, and far too faint. What first?
rounds.explain: With no sourness anywhere, the extraction is doing its job — there is simply not enough coffee in the water to taste. Move the ratio; grinding finer would start over-extracting what little is there.

rounds.prompt: Your espresso still tastes harsh. What would you try first?
rounds.explain: When grind and freshness are already right, harsh and rubbery usually traces back to the bean itself — swap it.

rounds.scenario: The bag was opened six weeks ago.
rounds.prompt: Nothing tastes wrong — it just tastes like nothing. What first?
rounds.explain: Flat and lifeless is staling, not extraction. No dial-in puts back aromatics that have already gone — start with fresher beans.

rounds.scenario: The shot ran 18 seconds and poured pale and fast.
rounds.prompt: It tastes sharp and thin. What first?
rounds.explain: A fast, pale, sour shot is under-extraction at espresso speed. Finer grounds add resistance and buy the water time. Tamping harder is the classic wrong move — tamp pressure barely changes flow once the bed is compact.

rounds.scenario: Grind unchanged since yesterday’s good shots.
rounds.prompt: The stream spits sideways and the cup tastes sour AND bitter at once. What first?
rounds.explain: Sour and bitter together is channeling — water racing through cracks while over-working the rest. That’s a prep fault, not a grind fault: grinding finer just channels harder.

rounds.scenario: The shot took 45 seconds and came out in slow drips.
rounds.prompt: Dry, harsh, lingering finish. What first?
rounds.explain: A choked, dripping shot over-extracts — coarser grounds open the bed back up. Cooler water treats the symptom and dulls the sweetness with it.

rounds.scenario: Timing is right at 28 seconds; nothing tastes off.
rounds.prompt: Balanced but overwhelming — like a punch in a thimble. What first?

choices.t: Let more run into the cup

rounds.explain: When the shot is balanced, extraction is done — what’s left is strength, and strength is the ratio: let more run into the cup. Grinding coarser speeds the flow and turns it sour; pulling it shorter makes it MORE intense, not less.

rounds.scenario: Dialled in, but the bag was roasted two months ago.
rounds.prompt: Crema vanishes in seconds and the shot tastes dull. What first?
rounds.explain: Crema is CO₂ from roasting — an old bag has already breathed it out, and no dial puts it back. Grinding finer fakes a slower shot but the gas is gone.

rounds.prompt: How fine should you grind for espresso?
rounds.feedback: Espresso lives at the fine end, just above powder. Too fine and the machine chokes; too coarse and the shot gushes.

rounds.prompt: And how coarse for a French press?
rounds.feedback: Four minutes of full immersion needs the coarsest setting on the dial — anything finer over-extracts and muddies the cup.

rounds.prompt: What brew ratio for a filter cup?
rounds.feedback: Most filter recipes land near 1:16. Pick one, weigh it, and change a single thing at a time from there.

rounds.prompt: How hot should the brew water be?
rounds.feedback: Just off the boil, around 93 to 96 °C. A rolling boil scorches the bed; much cooler and the sweetness never comes out.

rounds.prompt: How long should a single pour-over run?
rounds.feedback: Three to three and a half minutes, start to drawdown. Much faster is under-extracted; much slower means the bed has clogged.

rounds.prompt: How coarse for a pour-over?
rounds.feedback: Sea-salt territory. A few minutes of water passing through wants a medium-coarse bed — finer clogs the drawdown, coarser runs thin.

rounds.prompt: And for a moka pot?
rounds.feedback: Table salt — finer than pour-over but NOT espresso-fine. True espresso grind chokes a moka and turns it bitter.

rounds.prompt: How long is water in contact with espresso grounds?
rounds.feedback: About 28 seconds — the shortest contact time of any brewer, which is exactly why it takes the finest grind.

rounds.prompt: How coarse for cold brew?
rounds.feedback: The far coarse end — at or past French press. Twelve or more hours of steeping is the longest contact time there is, so the grind goes coarsest of all.

rounds.prompt: How long does a French press steep?
rounds.feedback: Around four minutes of full immersion — long contact, hence the coarsest everyday grind. Shorter tastes thin; much longer turns muddy and bitter.
